# Grammar of graphics

## ggplot2 builds a chart from parts

The **grammar of graphics** describes any chart by the same parts. ggplot2 gives each part its own function.

::: {.small}
| Part | Decides | In ggplot2 | Deck |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data | Which tibble to plot | `ggplot(data)` | 06 |
| Aesthetic mappings | Which column becomes x, y, colour, or size | `aes()` | 06 |
| Geoms | What draws the data: points, lines, bars | `geom_*()` | 06 |
| Stats | What a geom computes: counts, fitted lines | built into `geom_*()` | 06 |
| Positions | Where overlapping bars go | `position =` | 06 |
| Scales | How values become axes and colours | `scale_*()` | 08 |
| Coordinates | The plotting area | `coord_*()` | 08 |
| Facets | One panel per group | `facet_wrap()` | 08 |
| Themes | The look that is not data | `theme_*()` | 08 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,46,23,9]"}
:::

::: {.notes}
- Leland Wilkinson set out the grammar in *The Grammar of Graphics* (1999). ggplot2 follows Hadley Wickham's version, "A layered grammar of graphics" (2010).
- The table is for reference. This deck covers the first five rows; deck 08 covers the rest.
:::

## A chart maps columns to visual properties

```{r}
#| label: template
#| eval: false
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = column1, y = column2), data = my_tibble)
```

- `ggplot()`: an empty chart. `+` adds layers.
- `geom_*()`: the **geometry** that draws the data: points, lines, bars.
- `aes()`: **aesthetic mappings** from columns to visual properties (*aesthetics*): x, y, colour, size, fill.
- `data =`: the tibble to plot. Name it: a `geom_*()` takes the mapping first.

::: {.notes}
- Swapping the order, `geom_point(van17, aes(...))`, fails with "`mapping` must be created by `aes()`. ✖ You've supplied a data frame."
:::

## Change one part, get a different chart

```{r}
#| label: trend
#| include: false
trend <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", act_use_cat == "S/F Res",
         year(sale_date) %in% 2000:2025) |>
  group_by(year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(price = median(price) / 1e6)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: trend-point
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trend,
       aes(year, price)) +
  geom_point()
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: trend-line
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trend,
       aes(year, price)) +
  geom_line()
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: trend-col
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(trend,
       aes(year, price)) +
  geom_col()
```
:::
:::
::::

Same data, same mapping; only the geom changes. `trend` holds the median single-family price in Vancouver each year, in millions of dollars. ggplot2 has no function for a "line chart": you choose the parts.

::: {.notes}
- `trend` comes from `bca |> filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", act_use_cat == "S/F Res", year(sale_date) %in% 2000:2025) |> group_by(year = year(sale_date)) |> summarise(price = median(price) / 1e6)`.
:::

# Mappings

## A smaller dataset: Vancouver in 2017

```{r}
#| label: van17
van17 <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) == 2017) |>
  mutate(price_m = price / 1e6)
nrow(van17)
```

Most charts in this deck use `van17`, one city in one year, instead of all 1.3 million sales. `price_m` is the price in millions of dollars.

## geom_point() shows a relationship

```{r}
#| label: point
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(floorarea, price_m), data = van17)
```

## Map another column to colour

```{r}
#| label: colour
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(floorarea, price_m, colour = act_use_cat), data = van17)
```

Condos (`Strata Res`) are smaller and cheaper than houses (`S/F Res`).

## Mapping and setting are different

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: mapped
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(floorarea, price_m,
        colour = "blue"),
    data = van17)
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: set
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(floorarea, price_m),
    colour = "blue",
    data = van17)
```
:::
::::

Inside `aes()`, `"blue"` is treated as data, like `act_use_cat` on the last slide: ggplot2 maps it to a default colour and adds a legend. Outside `aes()`, it sets the colour.

## Set other visual properties: alpha, size, shape, linewidth

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: alpha
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(floorarea, price_m),
    alpha = 0.1,
    data = van17)
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
| Set it with | Changes |
|---|---|
| `alpha = 0.1` | Transparency, from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid) |
| `size = 0.5` | Point size |
| `shape = 1` | Point shape (1 is an open circle) |
| `linewidth = 1` | Line width, for `geom_line()` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[38,62]"}
:::
:::
::::

With `alpha`, the dense area shows. Each one can also go inside `aes()` to map a column, as `colour` did.

# Layers

## Layers stack: lines and points

```{r}
#| label: lines
#| fig-height: 2.4
avg_price <- bca |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat), data = avg_price) +
  geom_point(aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat), data = avg_price)
```

Each layer has its own mapping and data, so we write both twice.

## Global and local mappings

```{r}
#| label: global
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(avg_price, aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```

The same chart as the last slide. Data and `aes()` in `ggplot()` are **global**: every layer uses them, so you write them once. In a `geom_*()`, as on the last slide, they are **local**: only that layer uses them.

::: {.notes}
- `ggplot()` takes the data first; a `geom_*()` takes the mapping first. A layer usually reuses the plot's data but needs its own mapping.
:::

## ggplot() takes the data first, so you can pipe into it

```{r}
#| label: pipe
#| fig-height: 2.4
avg_price |>
  filter(act_use_cat == "Strata Res") |>
  ggplot(aes(sale_year, avg_price)) +
  geom_line()
```

`|>` passes the filtered rows to `ggplot()` as its data, so you do not have to name a new tibble. After `ggplot()`, add layers with `+`, not `|>`.

::: {.notes}
- `ggplot(...) |> geom_line()` fails with "`mapping` must be created by `aes()`. ✖ You've supplied a <ggplot2::ggplot> object. ℹ Did you use `%>%` or `|>` instead of `+`?"
:::

## geom_line() joins the points within each group

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: local
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(avg_price,
       aes(sale_year, avg_price)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(colour = "blue")
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: group
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(avg_price,
       aes(sale_year, avg_price)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_point(colour = "blue")
```
:::
::::

Left: with no groups, the line joins every point in year order. Right: `group` splits the line, as `group_by()` splits rows. Two slides back, `colour` did the same: a text column in `colour` also sets the group.

::: {.notes}
- A numeric column in `colour` does not set the group, so it does not split the line.
- ggplot2 groups by every discrete column mapped in the layer: `colour`, `fill`, `linetype`, `shape`, and `group`.
:::

## geom_smooth() draws a fitted line

```{r}
#| label: smooth
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

`geom_smooth()` computes a line that fits the points, then draws it. `method = "lm"` makes it a straight line, a regression line (deck 17). Like `geom_line()`, it draws one line for each group.

::: {.notes}
- Without `method = "lm"`, `geom_smooth()` draws a curve and prints which method it chose.
- The grey band around the line shows its uncertainty. With 11,000 sales it is too narrow to see.
:::

## Quick check: how many fitted lines?

```{r}
#| label: quiz-local
#| eval: false
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = act_use_cat), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

**A.** One  **B.** Two, one for each property type

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: quiz-local-answer
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = act_use_cat), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

**A.** `colour` is local to `geom_point()`, so `geom_smooth()` has one group and fits one line to all the points. Move `colour` into `ggplot()` to get one line per type.
:::

# Geoms

## Choose the geometry for the question

| Question | Geometry |
|---|---|
| How are two numbers related? | `geom_point()` |
| How does a value change over time? | `geom_line()` |
| How do groups compare? | `geom_col()` for values you computed, `geom_bar()` to count rows |
| How is one number distributed? | `geom_histogram()` |

## geom_bar() counts the rows for you

```{r}
#| label: bar-count
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(van17, aes(y = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_bar()
```

`geom_bar()` counts the rows in each group, then draws the counts. Its axis says `count`, a column it computed.

## geom_col() draws counts you computed

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: count
type_counts <- van17 |>
  count(act_use_cat)
type_counts
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: col-count
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(type_counts,
       aes(n, act_use_cat)) +
  geom_col()
```
:::
::::

`geom_col()` draws the `n` that `count()` computed, so the chart matches the last slide. `count()` is a shortcut for `group_by()` and `summarise(n = n())` from deck 05.

::: {.notes}
- With a pipe, `van17 |> count(act_use_cat) |> ggplot(aes(n, act_use_cat)) + geom_col()` draws the same chart without naming `type_counts`.
:::

## Some geoms compute what they draw

| Geom | Computes before drawing |
|---|---|
| `geom_bar()` | The number of rows in each group |
| `geom_histogram()` | Bins, then the number of rows in each bin |
| `geom_smooth()` | A fitted line, as in the quick check |
| `geom_boxplot()` | The median and quartiles |
| `geom_col()`, `geom_point()`, `geom_line()` | Nothing: they draw the values as given |

::: {.key-point}
When a geom computes, ask what it computed. `geom_bar()` counts rows, not people (deck 09).
:::

::: {.notes}
- `geom_bar(stat = "identity")` is the same as `geom_col()`. AI-written and older code often uses it.
- `after_stat(count)`, or the older `..count..`, refers to a column the geom computed.
- `geom_bar(aes(x, y))` fails with "`stat_count()` must only have an x or y aesthetic": `geom_bar()` computes y itself.
:::

## Vancouver sales by year and type

```{r}
#| label: van-sales
van_sales <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver",
         year(sale_date) %in% 2015:2025) |>
  count(year = year(sale_date), act_use_cat)
van_sales |> head(4)
```

`van_sales` has one row per year and property type. `n` is the number of sales.

## Bars stack by default

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: stack
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(van_sales,
       aes(year, n, fill = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_col()
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: dodge
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(van_sales,
       aes(year, n, fill = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge")
```
:::
::::

Left: the stack shows totals, but the top segments start at different heights, so single-family sales are hard to compare. Right: `position = "dodge"` starts every bar at zero.

::: {.notes}
`act_use_cat` is text, so the legend and the stack follow alphabetical order. As a factor, they would follow its levels (deck 08).
:::

## position = "fill" turns counts into shares

```{r}
#| label: fill
#| fig-height: 2
ggplot(van_sales, aes(year, n, fill = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill")
```

Each bar now sums to 1: shares, not counts. The axis still says `n`, and nothing warns you. Label it yourself (deck 08 explains `scale_*()`):

```{r}
#| label: fill-labels
#| eval: false
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(y = "Share of sales")
```

## Quick check: shares or counts?

```{r}
#| label: quiz-numbers
#| include: false
van_wide <- van_sales |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = act_use_cat, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(strata_share = round(100 * `Strata Res` / (`Strata Res` + `S/F Res`)))
pick <- \(y, col) van_wide[[col]][van_wide$year == y]
```

On the last chart, strata's share of Vancouver sales rose from `r pick(2016, "strata_share")`% in 2016 to `r pick(2019, "strata_share")`% in 2019. Did the number of strata sales rise?

**A.** Yes  **B.** The chart cannot tell you

::: {.fragment}
**B.** A share can rise while the count falls. Strata sales fell from `r scales::comma(pick(2016, "Strata Res"))` to `r scales::comma(pick(2019, "Strata Res"))`, but single-family sales fell faster, from `r scales::comma(pick(2016, "S/F Res"))` to `r scales::comma(pick(2019, "S/F Res"))`. To compare counts, use `position = "dodge"`.
:::

## Look up what a geom draws

| Resource | Use it to |
|---|---|
| [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html) ([PDF](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf)) | See every geom as a small picture |
| [ggplot2 reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/) | Read one function's arguments and example charts |
| [R Graph Gallery](https://r-graph-gallery.com/) | Find a chart type and see working code |
| [From Data to Viz](https://www.data-to-viz.com/) | Choose a chart from the kind of data you have |

In Positron, `?geom_histogram` opens the help page, and `example(geom_histogram)` draws its examples.

**Try it:** pick a geom from the cheat sheet that we have not used, read its page, and draw it with `van17`.

# Practice: price per square foot

## Practice (AI on)

For the City of Vancouver, plot the median price per square foot (`price / floorarea`) in each year from 2000 to 2025, with one line for each `act_use_cat`.

Try writing it yourself first, for five minutes. It doesn't have to run.

::: {.notes}
- Time the five minutes. Then everyone moves on to the agent, whether or not their code runs.
- Ask two or three students to show their attempts before anyone runs the agent.
- Look for a chart with no `colour` or `group` mapping (question 1), and for `median(price) / median(floorarea)`, which divides two medians: a different number from the median of each sale's price per square foot. Leave them; the first comes back on the reading slide, and the second is worth a minute of discussion.
:::

## Give the task to your agent

::: {.small}
```text
Create scripts/ggplot_1.qmd. From data/bca262.rds, compute the median
price per square foot (price / floorarea) of City of Vancouver sales in
each year from 2000 to 2025, for each act_use_cat. Draw it as a line
chart with one line for each act_use_cat.
```
:::

Run the code it writes. Then read it before you go on.

::: {.notes}
- Tested once on 2026-10-22 with Claude Code (Opus 5.5) in a fresh copy of the student folder: 4.4 minutes, the same chart as the answer slide, and no stop to ask.
  - It dropped sales with missing or zero floor area with `filter()` before computing (6,856 of 281,439 sales), so its `median()` has no `na.rm`. Question 2 covers either version.
  - Unasked, it reported that 13–19% of single-family sales have no floor area in 2005–2012 and 9–14% in 2017–18, and that this may bias those years' medians. That answers question 4; ask students whether they would have checked it themselves.
  - It used `.by =`, `between()`, `pivot_wider()`, and `slice_max()`, mostly to put numbers into its commentary, and explained each. Students should read the summary and the chart code closely and can skim the rest.
  - Its commentary offered land as one explanation for the single-family line, as on the answer slide, and mentioned the 2016 foreign buyers tax and the 2018 mortgage stress test.
- If an agent asks what to do with missing floor areas, let students choose; question 4 comes back to it.
:::

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: ppsf
#| fig-height: 2.2
van_rows <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) %in% 2000:2025) |>
  mutate(ppsf = price / floorarea)

van_ppsf <- van_rows |>
  group_by(year = year(sale_date), act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(median_ppsf = median(ppsf, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(van_ppsf, aes(year, median_ppsf, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line()
```
:::

::: {.notes}
- From 2000 to 2012, a condo sold for more per square foot than a house. Since 2013 the lines have traded places. Ask students why. One idea to test: a house's price pays for its land too.
:::

## Read the agent's code (AI off)

Compare the agent's code with yours. Where does it differ, and why? Then answer without asking the agent, editing and running the code yourself.

1. Remove the mapping that splits the lines (`colour =` or `group =`). Predict the chart, then run it.
2. Remove the step that handles missing floor areas: `na.rm = TRUE`, or a `filter()` on `floorarea`. Predict: an error, a warning, or a different chart?
3. Change `median()` to `mean()`. Which years jump? Find the sales behind them.
4. In which years do many single-family sales have no floor area? Did the agent tell you?

```{r}
#| label: ppsf-numbers
#| include: false
sf_ppsf <- van_rows |>
  filter(act_use_cat == "S/F Res") |>
  group_by(year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(med = median(ppsf, na.rm = TRUE), avg = mean(ppsf, na.rm = TRUE))
pm <- \(y, col) round(sf_ppsf[[col]][sf_ppsf$year == y])
```

::: {.notes}
- Question 1: one line zigzags between the two types every year, with no warning.
- Question 2: a warning about removed rows, and an almost empty chart. `median()` returns `NA` if any value is missing, and almost every year has a missing floor area.
- Question 3: single-family 2013 jumps from `r pm(2013, "med")` to `r pm(2013, "avg")`, and 2004 from `r pm(2004, "med")` to `r pm(2004, "avg")`, because of sales recorded at 1 or 2 sq ft. If the code keeps a floor area of 0, 2022 becomes `Inf`, and ggplot draws `Inf` at the top edge, where it looks like a real value. The tested agent dropped it.
- Question 4: `AGENTS.md` warns about 2005–2012. 2017 has a gap of the same size, which it does not mention.
:::

## Answer: no groups

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: ppsf-no-groups
#| fig-height: 2.4
# 1. One line through both types: it zigzags between them each year
ggplot(van_ppsf, aes(year, median_ppsf)) +
  geom_line()
```

## Answer: missing values left in

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: ppsf-no-narm
#| fig-height: 2.2
# 2. median() returns NA if any value is missing, so most points are gone.
#    ggplot warns that it removed rows, and draws what is left
van_rows |>
  group_by(year = year(sale_date), act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(median_ppsf = median(ppsf), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, median_ppsf, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line()
```
:::

## Answer: sales that pull the mean

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: ppsf-mean
# 3. Floor areas of 1 and 2 sq ft lift 2004 and 2013. A floor area of 0,
#    if kept, gives Inf in 2022, which ggplot draws at the top edge
van_rows |>
  arrange(desc(ppsf)) |>
  select(sale_date, act_use_cat, price, floorarea, ppsf) |>
  head(4)
```
:::

The median ignores a few extreme values. The mean does not, so check the extremes before you average.

## Answer: missing floor areas

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: ppsf-missing
# 4. Years in which more than 1 in 10 single-family sales has no floor area
van_rows |>
  filter(act_use_cat == "S/F Res") |>
  group_by(year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(no_floorarea = sum(is.na(floorarea)),
            share = mean(is.na(floorarea))) |>
  filter(share > 0.1)
```
:::

# Practice: Surrey sales by type

## Practice (AI on)

For the City of Surrey, count the sales of each `act_use_cat` in each year from 2015 to 2025. Draw a bar chart that shows how single-family sales changed.

Try writing it yourself first, for five minutes. It doesn't have to run.

::: {.notes}
- Time the five minutes, as before.
- Look for `geom_bar()` with both `x` and `y`, which fails with "`stat_count()` must only have an x or y aesthetic", and for stacked bars, which make single-family sales hard to compare (question 1).
:::

## Give the task to your agent

::: {.small}
```text
In scripts/ggplot_1.qmd, count the City of Surrey sales of each
act_use_cat in each year from 2015 to 2025. Draw a bar chart that shows
how single-family sales changed.
```
:::

Run the code it writes. Then read it before you go on.

::: {.notes}
- Tested once on 2026-10-22, continuing the same session: 1.3 minutes. It drew single-family bars only (`filter()`, then `geom_col()`), printed a table of both types, and noted that single-family fell from 55% to 20% of Surrey's sales. Question 1 asks students to put both types in one chart.
  - Unasked, it explained why `geom_col()` and not `geom_bar()`, and flagged that `S/F Res` in Surrey includes houses with suites (40% of the category's 2015–2025 sales) and duplexes (3%). Both checked.
- Other agents may choose `position = "dodge"` or facets. Each answers the task.
:::

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: surrey
#| fig-height: 2.4
surrey_sales <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Surrey", year(sale_date) %in% 2015:2025) |>
  count(year = year(sale_date), act_use_cat)

ggplot(surrey_sales, aes(year, n, fill = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge")
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: surrey-numbers
#| include: false
surrey_wide <- surrey_sales |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = act_use_cat, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(strata_share = round(100 * `Strata Res` / (`Strata Res` + `S/F Res`)))
sur <- \(y, col) surrey_wide[[col]][surrey_wide$year == y]
```

::: {.notes}
- Single-family sales fell from `r scales::comma(sur(2016, "S/F Res"))` in 2016 to `r scales::comma(sur(2025, "S/F Res"))` in 2025, while strata sales held up. Strata went from `r sur(2015, "strata_share")`% of Surrey's sales in 2015 to `r sur(2025, "strata_share")`% in 2025. Ask students what could explain it.
:::

## Read the agent's code (AI off)

Compare the agent's code with yours. Where does it differ, and why? Then answer without asking the agent, editing and running the code yourself.

1. Put both types in one chart with `fill = act_use_cat`. Try the bars stacked (the default), side by side (`"dodge"`), and as shares (`"fill"`). Which shows the change in single-family sales best?
2. Another agent counted the sales of both types, then drew `geom_bar(aes(year, fill = act_use_cat))` instead of `geom_col()`. Predict the chart, then run it.
3. Change the years to 2015–2026. What do the 2026 bars suggest? Is it true?
4. Count Surrey's single-family sales in 2025 yourself, with `filter()` and `nrow()`. Does the agent's bar match?

::: {.notes}
- Question 1: stacked, the single-family segments start at different heights. As shares, the chart cannot say whether single-family sales fell or strata sales rose, as in the quick check.
- Question 2: every bar is 2 high, with no error and no warning. `geom_bar()` counts the rows of the counted tibble: one per type and year.
- Question 3: 2026 looks like a collapse, but sales end on 11 March 2026. The student `AGENTS.md` should make the agent flag it.
:::

## Answer: geom_bar() on counted rows

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: surrey-bar
#| fig-height: 2.4
# 2. geom_bar() counts the rows of surrey_sales: one per type and year.
#    Every bar is 2 high, with no error and no warning
ggplot(surrey_sales, aes(year, fill = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_bar()
```

## Answer: 2026 and a check by hand

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: surrey-2026
# 3. Sales end on 11 March 2026, so the 2026 bars cover ten weeks
max(bca$sale_date)
bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Surrey", year(sale_date) == 2026) |>
  count(act_use_cat)

# 4. Single-family sales in Surrey in 2025
bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Surrey", year(sale_date) == 2025,
         act_use_cat == "S/F Res") |>
  nrow()
```
:::
